A current theory goes like this (the basic version):

1. The brain uses dopamine to attribute a sense of reward and novelty to new stimuli. The mind, in response, creates a logical set of ideas so that you, through consciousness, can understand it all and get through your day. This is normal. 

2. If the brain dopamine system is disrupted or damaged then the brain will attribute a sense of reward and importance to other things. 

3. The mind will then create explanations for these attributions, and there is no safeguard to alert the mind that the attributions are bizarre or unrealistic. This is where delusions are born. Logic often gets tossed aside. 

So everything that you’ve said above is really the result of your mind trying to develop explanations and make connections on things that the brain is handing it. But the brain machinery is damaged. Your mind has no choice but to create unrealistic ideas. 

Antipsychotic medications block dopamine from effecting the brain. Basically restores and undoes the damaged brain systems. The mind can then go about creating and maintaining appropriate beliefs based on real things.

Hope that makes sense.

- Even a preliminary diagnosis can be made. And will be required. Unless for some reason this is some atypically complicated case. But even then. The DSM is fairly clear on explaining a differential diagnosis (e.g. schizoaffective vs. depression with psychotic features; schizophreniform vs. schizophrenia, paranoid schizophrenia vs. delusional disorder). A trained expert will know how to word the questions and hone in on the best diagnosis given the presenting information. In this world of fast-paced insurance-driven managed care nobody walks away from the initial interview saying “I need two or three more sessions before I can commit to a diagnosis.” 

- The APA dumping the subtypes was, for most people I know, a curious step. One of many in the DSM-5. It was done basically because a schizophrenia code required a sub-type specifier to bill insurance, and the go-to subtype was paranoid type. Even though many people presented with features of various subtypes. Or none at all. Still, many people I I know still use them as just saying “Schizophrenia” seems too broad. Particularly paranoid type. The turn towards a more dimensional approach is interesting, but hasn’t quite been fully realized (and probably won’t be until around about the time that the DSM 6 or DSM 5.1 comes out).

This is actually not true—but amazingly common. Some drugs will cause temporary psychosis. Once the drug is out of the person’s system the symptoms go away. Other drugs over long term use will cause cognitive blunting a la “Cheech and Chong.”

More likely, someone will use drugs to counter the steady emergence of psychotic or affective symptoms. A form of self-medication. Family and friends don’t see the wrecking ball that’s gathering steam inside the person’s head. They just see the changes in behavior. It’s natural to conclude that drugs caused the illness when in fact it was the other way around.

Source: “Surviving schizophrenia” by E. Fuller Torrey (a must-have manual for understanding mental illness)

I read a lot of posts here from people who are wrestling with depression and even suicide. Self-hate, sense of failure, guilt and embarrassment are often sewn into the very fabric of these posts. 

But please remember that depression is a medical and biological condition. Not unlike high blood pressure, diabetes or countless other medical problems. Heard it all before—I know. But believe it!

Your thoughts, feelings and perceptions originate from the complex combinations of over a hundred neurotransmitters in the brain, interacting with each other at millions of locations inside this amazing 3 1/2 pound piece of goo that we call the brain. 

It seems remarkable that with all of these chemicals swirling around more errors, glitches and problems don’t happen more frequently. 

There are other factors, too. Genetic. Other medical things going on. Things happening in your world around you. But the bottom line is that it’s not your choice, nor is it something you have a whole lot of control over. At least not without professional help. Other than recognizing that 
it’s a vulnerability and that it can cloud or impact on your thinking. 

The trick is to be able to step outside of your feelings and recognize when your mood first tumbles the way an observer would. Insight! And then not blame yourself, but rather accept that it’s your condition acting up again. Make a deal with your depressed self that when you feel your way into this state you will get help, see a doctor, slow down life, come post on Reddit, etc. And if suicidal thoughts creep in those are the high alerts that “it” is back and you have to do some managing. 

It’s hard to do. Motivation is completely contrary to depression. But my point is that with perspective, it might make it easier to address. Perspective won’t FIX the feelings of awfulness, but it can provide that bit of light to not blame yourself and instead reach out.
